court: Office of Hearings and Appeals — Director's Decisions (U.S. Dept. of the Interior)
title: 43 OHA 236 — IN RE SHUGERT
text:
IN THE MATTER OF MATTHEW SHUGERT
DIR-2011-0073 Decided September 20, 2011
Appeal from an Administrative Wage Garnishment Notice issued by the U.S.
Department of the Treasury at the request of the National Operations Center, Bureau
of Land Management, U.S. Department of the Interior, finding former employee,
Matthew Shugert, financially liable for a debt in the amount of $1,408.29, Federal
Debt Case ID Number 2008084040A.
Affirmed, the debt to the United States is valid.
1. Administrative Wage Garnishment: Burden of Proof
In an administrative wage garnishment proceeding, the relevant
regulation, 31 C.F.R. §285.11(f)(8), requires that the agency has the
burden of going forward to prove the existence of the debt.
Thereafter, the debtor must establish by a preponderance of the
evidence that no debt exists or that the amount of the debt is
incorrect.
2. Property Board of Survey: Administrative Procedure: Administrative
Finality: Generally
A Board of Survey decision finding an employee negligent
and liable for loss of Government property becomes
administratively final when no appeal is filed from its
decision. Thereafter, the Department properly relies on the
findings and determination made by the Board of Survey.
3. Administrative Wage Garnishment: Burden of Proof: Preponderance of
the Evidence
Where the appellant/debtor fails to submit sufficient
evidence to rebut the agency case concerning the existence of

the debt, his appeal is properly denied and the validity of the
debt is affirmed.
APPEARANCES: Matthew Shugert, Pocatello, Idaho, pro se; Jacquelyn Miller,
Denver, Colorado, for the Bureau of Land Management.
OPINION BY HEARING OFFICIAL JAMES L. BYRNES
Introduction
Matthew Shugert (Appellant), a former employee with the U.S. Bureau of Land
Management (BLM), has appealed the June 11, 2010, Notice of Intent to Initiate
Administrative Wage Garnishment Proceedings (Notice) issued by the U.S.
Department of the Treasury. The Notice was issued pursuant to a request from BLM
dated April 29, 2008, requesting wage garnishment to satisfy a debt resulting from a
finding of gross negligence in the loss of Government equipment by the BLM
California State Office Board of Survey (Board). Appellant was advised that, as of
the date of the Notice, the amount of the debt was $1,408.29.
Appellant’s appeal was received by the Office of Hearings and Appeals on
July 18, 2011, and was assigned Docket No. DIR-2011-0073. BLM transmitted the
official file to this office on August 4, 2011. The file consists in pertinent part of: the
Report of Survey (BR-RS05-0002), signed by the Reviewing Official on May 7, 2005;
Form DI-105, Receipt for Property issued to and signed by Appellant; copies of cell
phone usage bills for the months of July, September, October, November and
December of 2004; and various memoranda, e-mail, bills for collection, and demand
letters related to the debt.
The record discloses that Appellant was hired by BLM in a career conditional
appointment on June 27, 2004. Beginning in October 2004, Appellant was alleged to
have been AWOL from his job on numerous occasions. Appellant’s employment with
BLM was terminated on November 12, 2004, according to BLM. However, Appellant
contends that he submitted a letter of resignation effective October 22, 2004.
In describing the loss of the items, Appellant’s former Supervisor submitted a
statement to the Board explaining that:
These items (King GPH5102X Radio; Nokia 8260 Cell Phone; and
keys to King Range Office) were issued to Matt Shugert when he was the
Supervisory Range Technician in charge of the King Ranch Fire Engine
Module. . . .

. . . . The Special Agent assigned to the Arcata Field Office
conducted an investigation and determined that Item #2 had phone calls
originating throughout the western US, up through 11/16/04. These items
listed above are expected to still be in the possession of Matt Shugert.
Statement to the Board, dated Mar. 11, 2005.
The Board of Survey Decision
In its findings, the Board stated:
Employee was employed as a Supervisory Range Technician in-
charge of the King Range Fire Engine Module and was issued the subject
Survey Report Equipment in support of his employment responsibilities.
Upon his termination, the Special Agent assigned to the Arcata Field Office
conducted a through investigation and determined that the employee not
only was in possession of the equipment, but, in the case of the cell phone,
was still utilizing it. . . .
In its recommendations, the Board concluded:
The Board finds that the employee illegally took the subject
equipment, and in the case of the cell phone, continued to use it for several
months after his termination. We find that the employee was responsible
for the property and liable for its loss. The Board finds that the liability for
the loss of this [G]overnment property rest[s] with the employee (now
terminated) and that this individual should be held financially responsible
to the Agency for the Fair Market Value of the missing property plus the
billed invoice value of all cell phone calls made after his termination . . . .
The Board found Appellant liable for loss of Government property and
unauthorized cell phone calls in the amount of $769.49. Appellant was notified by
letter dated September 27, 2005, that he had been found negligent and financially
liable for the equipment and the cell phone calls. However, Appellant did not avail
himself of the opportunity to appeal the decision. Subsequently, BLM prepared Bills
for Collection and Demand Letters which were served on the Appellant. When these
various communications went unanswered, BLM requested the U.S. Department of
the Treasury to initiate wage garnishment proceedings. The Notice was issued by the
U.S. Department of the Treasury dated June 11, 2010. Appellant filed a request for
hearing on the notice, dated July 8, 2011, with the U.S. Department of the Treasury.
It was filed with this Office on July 18, 2011. In his request, he stated: “[t]hrough

DIR-2011-0073
my investigation I found my former supervisor provided falsifide [sic] documentation
to BLM concerning this issue which lead [sic] to the garnishment.”
By Order dated August 29, 2011, I determined, consistent with 31 C.F.R.
§ 285.11(f)(2), that a written hearing would be sufficient to resolve this matter.
Appellant was given notice, pursuant to 31 C.F.R. § 285.11 (f)(7)(iii), that he had
until September 13, 2011, to submit any additional arguments, evidence, or exhibits.
Argument on Appeal
In response to the Order, Appellant provided his arguments and exhibits in a
submission dated September 7, 2011. Appellant contested the findings of the Board
of Survey and asserted that:
In 2006 I was informed there were serious issues with my
employment record relating to my former supervisor and employer,
California Bureau of Land Management, dating back to 2004. I was
informed my record did not reflect my resignation from [BLM] in
October 2004. Instead my record said I was terminated from my position
in November 2004. To make matters worse, there were accusations I had
stolen BLM property. Because of these issues I lost my career with the
federal government in 2006[.]
Since 2006 I have tried to resolve this serious problem. I have
continuously tried working with the [BLM], the Merit Systems Protection
Board and, in 2009, filed a case with the Office of Special Counsel. The
reason why this problem has never been resolved is because my former
supervisor has withheld evidence, provided falsified evidence, provided
falsified testimony and BLM as an agency has been unwilling to provide me
assistance.
. . . .
The newly recovered evidence provide[s] support for my claim that I
did not steal property from California BLM in 2004, and more importantly,
my former supervisor, Tim Jones, did knowingly provide false testimony
and falsified documents concerning this issue. . . .
. . . .
The last sentence . . . states “Matt Shugert has been charged with
Grand Theft with the state of California . . . This statement is false!

On December 12, 2004 a report was filed by BLM to the state
accusing me of Grand Theft of [G]overnment property.
Four weeks later on January 17, 2005 the District Attorney for the
Superior Court of California, Humboldt County rejected the case, Under
the Interest of Justice.
I was advised the report from BLM lacked any evidence of wrong
doing by me. The District Attorney could not and would not pursue any
charges against me.
. . . .
Property not turned in: (Property record)
There are major discrepancies with this document. The employers

the hand held radio I am accused of taking. In the Description Section it is

information added to it after it was signed by me. Tim Jones added “model

By comparing the two forms for this document it is obvious

Another fact about the Receipt for Property form is the date it was
signed, 09/02/04. I started my position in June 2004 but the form states I
did not get equipment assigned to me until September 2004.
. . . .

When comparing the signatures, take the top copy (Tim Jones’s
copy) and fold the paper at the signature and date section. By doing this,

You will clearly see the signature and dates do not match.
. . . .
In summary, I have proven the information provided by Tim Jones
in his report to the Board of Survey is false. The supporting evidence I

Tim Jones knowingly provided falsified and forged documents concerning

Hearing Statement, dated September 7, 2011.
Review of the Debt Validity
[1] In an administrative wage garnishment proceeding, the relevant regulation,
31 C.F.R. §285.11(f)(8), requires that the agency has the burden of going forward to
prove the existence of the debt. Thereafter, the debtor must establish by a
preponderance of the evidence that no debt exists or that the amount of the debt is
incorrect.
BLM has submitted a Receipt for Property signed by the Appellant on
September 2, 2004. Among the items listed are “Nokia G250 cell phone
707/498-7252” and “Property Number - 0429252 Bendix King Hand Held Radio,
GPH Model # 5102x Quantity 1 S/N 022008.” Also contained in the BLM record are
U.S. Cellular cell phone bills to BLM for the Nokia G250 cell phone, number
707/498-7252, dated July 18, 2004, September 18, 2004, October 18, 2004,
November 18, 2004, and December 18, 2004.
The foregoing items, along with the statements by Appellant’s former BLM
Supervisor regarding Appellant’s failure to return these items, were contained in the
record reviewed and relied upon by the California BLM Board of Survey in
determining the liability of the Appellant for the amount of the administrative wage
garnishment. After reviewing BLM’s record, I have determined that these
submissions, taken as a whole, are sufficient to meet BLM’s burden of establishing the
debt as valid. The record establishes that the Nokia G250 cell phone, number
707/498-7252, and the Bendix King Hand Held Radio were assigned to Appellant
and that he acknowledged such. The statements of Appellant’s Supervisor and the
decision of the Board of Survey also substantiate BLM’s allegation that Appellant
43 OHA 241

DIR-2011-0073
failed to return said items and continued to use the Nokia G250 cell phone, number
707/498-7252, for his personal use, including a period after he vacated his BLM
position. Therefore, the burden of proof in this proceeding shifts to the Appellant to
show, by a preponderance of evidence, that the debt is not valid.
[2] Appellant attempts a collateral attack on the decision of the California BLM
Board of Survey process, asserting variously that he was not informed of the
proceedings and that his Supervisor submitted “falsified and forged documentation”
to the Board, which caused the Board to issue an incorrect decision.
As evidence of being excluded from the proceedings, the Appellant has
submitted a copy of an envelope sent to his address, which was returned with the
notation “Return to Sender [-] Shugert, Matthew Moved Left No Address [-] Unable
To Forward [-] Return To Sender.” However, the address in question was the
Appellant’s address of record which he had on file with BLM. This Office has
consistently ruled that a person will be deemed to have received the communication
if it was delivered to his last address of record in the appropriate office of the Bureau
of Land Management, regardless of whether it was in fact received by him. See, e.g.,
Joel Carothers, 179 IBLA 244, 248-250 (2010); Arthur M. Solander, 79 IBLA 70, 73
(1984). BLM has issued a wide variety of letters, bills, and demand letters to the
Appellant in an attempt to resolve this debt. The fact that Appellant discontinued the
use of the address he had on file with BLM and failed to either submit a change of
address to BLM or file a forwarding request with the Postal Service is a defect of his
own making.
As noted above, the Board’s decision in this matter was issued in 2005.
Appellant’s collateral attack on its conclusion at this late date must fail since the
decision is considered settled under the doctrine of administrative finality. In re San
Tan Irrigation District, 30 OHA 1, 13-14 (2005). The doctrine of administrative
finality, the administrative counterpart of the doctrine of res judicata, dictates that
once a party has had an opportunity to obtain administrative review of an agency
decision within the Department and the decision has been upheld on appeal, the
decision may not be reconsidered in subsequent proceedings, except upon a showing
of compelling legal or equitable reasons. Gifford H. Allen, 131 IBLA 195, 202 (1994).
However, a precondition for the application of the principle of res judicata is that the
matter raised in the subsequent proceeding was one distinctly put in issue and
directly determined in the earlier litigation. State of Alaska, 140 IBLA 205, 211
(1997). The precise issue before the Board was Appellant’s liability for the debt in
question. Thus, BLM is entitled to rely on the Board’s decision in this matter in
making a determination of liability.
[3] Further, I have completed a review de novo of all the evidence submitted by
BLM and the Appellant and conclude that the Appellant has failed in his effort to
43 OHA 242

DIR-2011-0073
show the debt is not valid. Appellant makes numerous allegations of “falsified and
forged documents” and allegedly false statements made by his former BLM
Supervisor. However, the bulk of his allegations and accusations involve the issue of
the termination of his employment with California BLM. These issues are irrelevant
to this hearing, since the only issue I decide is the validity of the debt caused by the
failure to return the Nokia G250 cell phone, number 707/498-7252, and the Bendix
King Hand Held Radio upon the termination of his employment with BLM.
After a thorough review of Appellant’s submissions, I conclude that they are
neither credible nor persuasive. Appellant contends that his employee copy of the
September 2, 2004, DI-105 Receipt for Property, shows that the Bendix King Hand
Held Radio was never assigned to him. I disagree. The DI-105 clearly shows
19 items charged to Appellant’s care for use in his job. The radio is listed as Item 17
and its property number is clearly stated. Since the DI-105 was handwritten and
contains only items that were assigned, it is impossible to conclude that the radio was
not assigned to Appellant. While Appellant is correct that there were further
handwritten interlineations made to this entry on his former Supervisor’s copy,
possibly sometime after he signed it, they appear to have been made to clarify which
particular radio was missing. The Appellant’s signature is identical on both copies of
the DI-105. Therefore, the essential element of proof that the Bendix King Hand Held
Radio was actually assigned to him must be decided in favor of BLM. I note that
other than a general denial, Appellant has made no attempt to explain why this one
item on a DI-105, containing 18 other items, would be singled out as missing or how
this matter was handled during the check-out process.
As to the other portion of the debt in question, the Appellant was notably silent
regarding the disposition of Nokia G250 cell phone, number 707/498-7252. This
item is also clearly listed on the DI-105, demonstrating Appellant’s acknowledgment
that it was assigned to him for BLM job related use. The U.S. Cellular phone bill for
this phone, dated July 18, 2004, shows the total charges amounted to $28.13. The
charges for the bill dated September 18, 2004, show an amount due of $26.17.
However, the charges for the bill dated October 18, 2004, show a total amount
due of $554.73. A review of the individually billed phone calls reveals that,
consistent with BLM’s claims, these phone calls were placed from a variety of
locations throughout the western states and to a wide variety of phone numbers in
various states. This pattern is repeated on the bill dated November 18, 2004, with a
total amount due of $755.39. The same is true of the bill dated December 18, 2004,
with a due amount of $117.42.
Of particular note, one of the many addresses contained in the case file for
Appellant is an address in Mount Pleasant, Michigan. Appellant discloses in his filing
that this is his family’s address. Among the numerous phone calls made on the Nokia
43 OHA 243

DIR-2011-0073
G250 cell phone, number 707/498-7252, none of which seem to have any relevance
to his employment with BLM, are phone calls made to Mount Pleasant, Michigan.
Some of the calls were placed to cell phone numbers in Mount Pleasant. However,
there is a series of calls spread over the phones bills to 989/773-1533, a land line
phone number in Mount Pleasant, Michigan. I hereby take administrative notice that
a check of the internet White Pages phone book reveals that this number is related to
the Appellant in this matter. It therefore is unlikely that these calls were made by
anyone other than the Appellant. I conclude that BLM has established the validity of
the debt in the matter and that Appellant has failed to show he does not owe the
amount in question. Appellant is required to pay the amount requested by the U.S.
Department of the Treasury.
Based on the foregoing, I rule that the debt to the United States is valid. The
U.S. Department of the Treasury is requested to proceed with the administrative
wage garnishment.
This decision constitutes the final administrative determination of the
Department in this matter. 31 C.F.R. § 285.11(f)(12).
